subject: Archaeology
title: Astronomy in Babylon
description: A 60-second lesson on Astronomy in Babylon.

hook.text: Babylonian priests tracked the stars so precisely that they predicted eclipses centuries before the Greeks even tried.

buildup.text: Astronomical diaries recorded planetary positions nightly for over 700 years — the longest continuous scientific record.

discovery.text: The MUL.APIN tablets listed constellations, rising times, and seasonal markers that farmers and priests relied on.

twist.text: The zodiac — Aries, Taurus, Gemini — is a Babylonian invention. Greek astrology copied it almost directly.

climax.text: A 2016 study found Babylonians used geometric methods to track Jupiter — predating European calculus by 1,400 years.

punchline.text: Your horoscope sign was named by Babylonian priests.

quiz.question: What groundbreaking mathematical method did Babylonian astronomers use?
options: They invented the telescope to observe the planets more closely
They used geometric methods to track Jupiter, predating European calculus by 1,400 years
They developed a heliocentric model of the solar system

details.summary: Babylonian astronomers tracked planetary movements, predicted eclipses, and developed the zodiac system. Their meticulous observations recorded on clay tablets over centuries created the foundation for both Greek astronomy and modern astronomical science.
details.whyItMatters: Babylonian astronomy was the ancient world's most sophisticated. Their systematic observation and record-keeping established the scientific method in embryonic form, directly influencing Greek and later European science.
takeaways: Babylonians tracked planets and predicted eclipses accurately
They developed the zodiac system used in astronomy and astrology
Their records directly influenced Greek astronomical science

faq.question: How accurate were Babylonian astronomical predictions?
faq.answer: Remarkably accurate. By the 500s BCE, Babylonian astronomers could predict lunar eclipses to within hours. Their planetary observations, accumulated over centuries, were precise enough that Greek astronomers like Hipparchus relied on Babylonian data.

faq.question: Did the Babylonians invent the zodiac?
faq.answer: Yes. They divided the ecliptic into twelve equal segments, each named after a constellation, around the 5th century BCE. This system was adopted by Greek astronomers and eventually became the basis for both Western astronomical coordinates and astrological traditions.
